entries.summary: You can copy a published protocol into your own draft. The copy remembers which protocol and which published version it came from, leaves out anything the owner kept private, and editing it never changes the original.

On a saved lab report you can now confirm each result against your own report, mark it as possibly wrong, or withdraw it (after a confirmation); the page shows right away whether it counts in statistics.

The saved-report page now shows each result against its three ranges, kept separate: the laboratory reference range, the longevity-optimal range and the safety threshold, each with its status in words and its source; the optimal range's provenance opens in one click.
The page for typing a lab report by hand no longer says a saved report can be undone, and after you remove a result, focus moves to the next field and the removal is announced.
A page for importing lab results from a CSV file now lets you check each row, save only when all are recognised, and undo the import.
A plain-language user guide now lists what you can do today and what is still to come.
An architecture page now shows what is built and what is only planned.
A documentation section now opens with a page listing every place where AI writes words.
Automatic checks now test that the unit-conversion code is well covered by tests.
Automatic checks now enforce stricter typing on the terminology code.
Automatic checks now scan the code for common security mistakes.
Automatic checks now confirm that every specification is well formed.
A public Ecosystem page now shows what biohack.it builds on and what it gives back.
Automatic checks now look for known security problems in the backend libraries.
The web framework was upgraded to a patched release that fixes known security problems.
The project papers were compared with the specifications and the gaps were written down.
Automatic checks now require that changed backend code is well covered by tests.
